Not to me. They wanted to hide it from me, but I knew they were talking.
You'll grow used to hearing shameful things said of me. I suppose I shall grow used to it, too.
Ah, it's not that I mind. What torments me is that it was so easy to despise their praise, and now I can't despise their blame.
[Smiling.] I believe you have some glimmerings of human nature in you after all.
When you came to-night, so calm and self-possessed, I admired you as I'd never admired you before.

It's easy enough to command one's face. I learnt to do that in Africa when often my life depended on my seeming to have no fear. But in my heart ... I never knew that I could feel so bitter. And yet, after all, it's only your good opinion that I care for.
I've trusted you implicitly from the first day I saw you.
Thank God for that! To-day is the first time I've wanted to be assured that I was trusted. And yet I'm ashamed to want it.
Ah, don't be too hard upon yourself. You're so afraid of letting your tenderness appear.

The only way to be strong is never to surrender to one's weakness. Strength is merely a habit like everything else. I want you to be strong, too. I want you never to doubt me whatever you may hear said.
I gave my brother into your hands, and told you that if he died a brave man's death I could ask for no more.
I should tell you that I've made up my mind to make no answer to the charges that are made against me.
[There is a very short pause, while he looks at her steadily.

[To Lucy.] I can give you my word of honour that I've done nothing which I regret. I know that what I did was right with regard to George, and if it were all to come again I would do exactly as I did before.
I think I can trust you.
I thought of you always, and everything I did was for your sake. Every single act of mine during these four years in Africa has been done because I loved you.
You must love me always, Alec, for now I have only you. [He bends down and kisses her hand.] Come!
[He gives her his arm and they walk out.
I feel as if I should rather like to cry.
Do you really? So do I.
By the way, you don't want to dance with me, do you?
It's charming of you to say so. It puts me at my ease at once.
Come and sit on the sofa and talk seriously.
Ah, you want to flirt with me, Mrs. Crowley.
Good heavens, what on earth makes you think that?
It's what a woman always means when she asks you to talk sensibly.
I can't bear a man who thinks women are in love with him.
Bless you, I don't think that. I only think they want to marry me.

Not at all. However old, ugly, and generally undesirable a man is, he'll find a heap of charming girls who are willing to marry him. Marriage is still the only decent means of livelihood for a really nice girl.
But, my dear friend, if a woman really makes up her mind to marry a man, nothing on earth can save him.
Don't say that, you terrify me.
You need not be in the least alarmed, because I shall refuse you.
Thanks, awfully. But all the same I don't think I'll risk a proposal.
My dear Mr. Lomas, your only safety is in immediate flight.
It must be obvious to the meanest intelligence that you've been on the verge of proposing to me for the last month.
Oh, I assure you, you're quite mistaken.
Then I shan't come to the play with you to-morrow?
But I've taken the seats, and I've ordered an exquisite dinner at the Carlton.

lg.l: Potage Bisque... [She makes a little face.]
Sole Normande... [She shrugs her shoulders.]
Wild Duck.

div.p: And I've ordered a soufflé with an ice in the middle of it.
I shouldn't have thought you kept very well abreast of dramatic art if you insist on marrying every man who takes you to a theatre.
[Demurely.] I was very nicely brought up.
Of course, if you're going to make yourself systematically disagreeable unless I marry you, I suppose I shall have to do it in self-defence.
I don't know if you have the least idea what you're talking about. I'm sure I haven't!
I was merely asking you in a rather well-turned phrase to name the day. The lamb shall be ready for the slaughter!
Couldn't you infuse a little romance into it? You might begin by going down on your bended knees.
I assure you that's quite out of fashion. Lovers, nowadays, are much too middle-aged, and their joints are creaky. Besides, it ruins the trousers.
At all events, there can be no excuse for your not saying that you know you're utterly unworthy of me.
Wild horses wouldn't induce me to make a statement which is so remote from the truth.
And, of course, you must threaten to commit suicide if I don't consent.
Women are such sticklers for routine. They have no originality.
Very well, have it your own way. But I must have a proposal in due form.
Only four words are needed. [Counting them on his fingers.] Will you marry me?
That is both clear and simple. I reply in one: No!
[As though he were not sure that he had heard correctly.] I beg your pardon?
The answer is in the negative.
I will be a sister to you.
Do you mean to say you deliberately refuse me?
[With much seriousness.] I thank you from the bottom of my heart.
[Puzzled.] The man's mad. The man's nothing short of a raving lunatic.
I wanted to see if you were really attached to me. You have given me a proof of esteem which I promise you I will never forget.
[Laughing.] You're a perfect idiot, Mr. Lomas!
It's one of my cherished convictions that a really nice woman is never so cruel as to marry a man she cares for.
You're much too flippant to marry anybody, and you're perfectly odious into the bargain.
[She goes out. Dick, chuckling, lights a cigarette. Alec comes in and lies down lazily on the sofa.
Why, Dick, what's the matter? You look as pleased as Punch.
My dear fellow, I feel like the Terrible Turk. I've been wrestling, and I thought I was going to have a fall. But by the display of considerable agility I've managed to keep my legs.
Nothing. It's merely the gaiety of forty-two.
[Boulger comes into the room, followed immediately by Mallins and Carbery. He starts slightly when he sees Alec, but then goes over to the table on which is the whiskey.
Certainly. Dick insisted that this room should be particularly reserved for that purpose.
[The Butler comes in with a small silver salver, and takes up one or two dirty glasses.
Lady Kelsey is the most admirable of all hostesses.

[Taking a cigarette from his case.] Give me a match, Bobby, there's a good boy. [Boulger, with his back turned to Alec, takes no notice. He pours himself out some whiskey. Alec smiles slightly.] Bobby, throw me over the matches!
Mr. Mackenzie is asking for something.
You might give me a light, will you?
[The Butler takes the matches to Alec, who lights his cigarette.
Thank you. [Complete silence is preserved till the Butler leaves the room.] I perceive, Bobbie, that during my absence you have not added good manners to your other accomplishments.
If you want things, you can ask the servants for them.
Would you be so kind as to remember that my name is Boulger?
[Smiling.] Perhaps you would like me to call you Sir Robert?
I should prefer that you would call me nothing at all. I have absolutely no wish to know you.
Which shows that your taste is as bad as your breeding.
[Angrily, walking up to him.] By God, I'll knock you down!
You could hardly do that when I'm already lying on my back.
Look here, Mackenzie, I'm not going to let you play the fool with me. I want to know what answer you have to make to all these charges that have been brought against you.
Might I suggest that only Miss Allerton has the least right to receive answers to her questions? And she hasn't questioned me.

I've given up trying to understand her attitude. If I were she, it would make me sick with horror to look at you. Since this morning you've rested under a direct accusation of causing George's death, and you've said nothing in self-defence.
You've been given an opportunity to explain yourself, and you haven't taken it.
Are you not going to deny the charge?
Then I can only draw one conclusion. There appears to be no means of bringing you to justice, but at least I can refuse to know you.
All is over between us. And shall I return your letters and your photograph?
It's singular that though I'm Scotch and you are English I should be able to see how ridiculous you are, while you're quite blind to your own absurdity.
Come, Alec! Remember he's only a boy.

[To Dick Lomas.] I'm perfectly able to look after myself, and I'll thank you not to interfere. [To Alec.] If Lucy's so indifferent to her brother's death that she's willing to keep up with you, that's her own affair ...
[Interrupting.] Come, Bobbie, don't make a scene.
Do you think this is quite the place for an altercation? Wouldn't you gain more notoriety if you attacked me in my club or at Church parade on Sunday?

It's mere shameless impudence that you should come here to-night. You're using these wretched women as a shield, because you know that as long as Lucy sticks to you there are people who won't believe the story.
I came for the same reason as yourself, dear boy. Because I was invited.
I shan't shut up. The man's got no right to force himself here.
Remember that you're Lady Kelsey's nephew.
I didn't ask him. D'you think I'd have come if I knew he was going to be here? He's acknowledged that he has no defence.
Pardon me, I acknowledge nothing and deny nothing.
That won't do for me. I want the truth, and I'm going to get it. I've got a right to know.
[Beginning to lose his temper.] Don't make an ass of yourself, Bobby.
By God, I'll make you answer!
[As he says this he goes up to Alec furiously, but Alec. with a twist of his arm, hurls him back.
I could break your back, you silly boy.
[With a cry of anger Boulger is about to spring at Alec when Dick gets in the way.
Now then, no scenes. And you'll only get the worst of it, Bobby. Alec could just crumple you up. Take him away, Mallins. Don't stand there like a stuffed owl, Carbery.
Now then, be off with you. Don't make a silly ass of yourself.
Poor Lady Kelsey! To-morrow half London will be saying that you and Bobby had a stand-up fight in her drawing-room.
The position is growing confoundedly awkward!

They lick my boots till I loathe them, and then they turn against me like a pack of curs. Oh, I despise them—these silly boys who stay at home wallowing in their ease while men work. Thank God, I've done with them all now. They think one can fight one's way through Africa as easily as one walks down Piccadilly. They think one goes through hardships and dangers, illness and starvation, to be the lion of a dinner-party in Mayfair.
[With a visible effort containing himself completely, with studied nonchalance.] D'you think that I look wildly excited?
[Ironically.] I don't think butter would melt in your mouth.
[Dick and Alec go out into the garden. In a moment Boulger comes in with Lady Kelsey.
I think you're dreadfully foolish, Bobby. You know how Lucy resents any interference with her actions.
Won't you sit down? You must be dreadfully tired.
Why won't you wait till to-morrow?
I feel that it ought to be settled at once.
Did you send for me, my aunt? Mr. Carbery said you wanted to speak to me here.
Yes, I gave him that message.
I asked Aunt Alice to beg you to come here. I was afraid you wouldn't if I asked you.
[Lightly.] What nonsense! I'm always delighted to see you.
I wanted to speak to you about something, and I thought Aunt Alice should be present.
Is it so important that it can't wait till to-morrow?
I venture to think it's very important.
[He hesitates for a moment, then braces himself to the ordeal.
I've told you often, Lucy, that I've been in love with you for as many years as I can remember.
Surely you've not snatched me from the unwilling arm of my partner in order to make me a proposal of marriage?
[Smiling.] I assure you it doesn't suit you at all.
The other day I asked you again to marry me, just before Alec Mackenzie came back.
It was very charming of you. You mustn't think that because I laugh at you a little I'm not grateful for your affection.
Except for that letter in this morning's Times, I should never have dared to say anything to you again. But that changes everything.
I don't understand what you mean.
[After a little pause.] I ask you again if you'll be my wife? When Alec Mackenzie came back I understood why you were so indifferent to me, but you can't marry him now.
You have no right to talk to me like this.
I'm the only man who's related to you at all, and I love you with my whole soul.
I think you should listen to him, Lucy. I'm growing old, and soon you'll be quite alone in the world.
I don't ask you to care for me. I only want to serve you.
I can only repeat that I'm very grateful to you. I can never marry you.

[Beginning to lose his temper again.] Are you going to continue to know Mackenzie? If you'll take the advice of any unprejudiced person about that letter, you'll find that he'll say the same as I. There can be no shadow of doubt that Mackenzie is guilty of a monstrous crime.
I don't care what the evidence is. I know he can't have done a shameful thing.
But have you forgotten that it's your own brother he killed? The whole country is up in arms against him, and you are quite indifferent.
[Much moved.] Oh, Bobbie, how can you be so cruel?
If you ever really cared for George at all, you must wish to punish the man who caused his death.
Oh, why d'you torment me? I tell you that he isn't guilty. It's because I'm convinced of that ...
He might give you the truth.
It's very strange that he should insist on this silence.
Do you believe that story too?
I don't know what to believe. It's so extraordinary. If the man's innocent, why doesn't he speak?
He knows I trust him. I couldn't cause him the great pain of asking him questions.
Are you afraid he couldn't answer them?
Well, just try. After all, you owe as much as that to the memory of George.
I think it's very unreasonable, Lucy. He knows we're his friends. He can count on our discretion.
I believe in him implicitly. I believe in him with all the strength I've got.
Then, surely it can make no difference if you ask him. There can be no reason for him not to trust you.
Oh, why don't you leave me alone?
Ask him point blank. If he refuses to answer you ...

[Hastily.] It would mean nothing. Why should he answer? I believe in him absolutely. I think he's the greatest and most honourable man I've ever known. I care more for his little finger than for the whole world. I love him with all my heart. And that's why he can't be guilty of this horrible crime. Because I've loved him for years, and he's known it. And he loves me. And he's loved me always.
[Alec and Dick stroll in from the garden.
Alec, Alec, I want you! Thank God, you've come!
[Going to her quickly.] What is it?
Alec, you must tell them now about you and me.
[Alec looks at Lucy for a moment, and then turns to Lady Kelsey.
I think perhaps we ought to have told you before, Lady Kelsey. But we wanted to enjoy our little secret by ourselves.
I have asked Lucy to be my wife, and she....
[Interrupting him.] She said she would be honoured and deeply grateful.
[Greatly embarrassed.] I hardly know what to say.... How long have you been engaged?
Won't you tell me you're pleased, my aunt? I know you want me to be happy.
Of course, I want you to be happy. But I—I....
[Boulger turns on his heel and walks out.
[Offering his arm to Lady Kelsey.] Wouldn't you like to go back to the drawing-room?

lg.l: [She allows herself to be led away, helplessly.
Alec and Lucy are left alone.

div.p: [With a smile.] I don't think our announcement has been received with enthusiasm.
You're not angry with me, Alec?
Of course not. Everything you do is right and charming.
I shall really think I'm a wonderful person if I've taught you to pay compliments.
I'm so glad to be alone with you. Now, at all events, people will have the sense to leave us by ourselves.
[Passionately.] I want your love. I want your love so badly.
[Taking her in his arms.] My darling!
[Clinging to him.] The moment I'm with you I feel so confident and happy.
Only when you're with me? [Lucy looks at him for an instant. He repeats the question in a caressing voice.] Only when you're with me, darling?
Why d'you think I made you tell them we were engaged?
I had to tell them. I couldn't keep it back. They made me suffer so dreadfully.
The brutes! Tell me what they did.
Oh, they said horrible things about you.
It's nothing to you. But to me.... Oh, you don't know what agony I endure. I'm such a coward! I thought I was so much braver.

I wanted to burn my ships behind me. I wanted to reassure myself. [Alec makes a slight movement away from her, but she holds him back anxiously.] Forgive me, dear. You don't know how terrible it is. I stand so dreadfully alone. Every one is convinced that you caused poor George's death—every one but me. [Alec looks at her gravely, without speaking.] I try to put the thoughts out of my head, but I can't—I can't. That letter in the Times looks so dreadfully true. Don't you see what I mean? The uncertainty is more than I can bear. At the first moment I felt so absolutely sure of you.
I trust you just as much as ever. I know it's impossible that you should have done a shameful thing. But there it stands in black and white, and you have nothing to say in answer.
I know it's very difficult. That is why I asked you to believe in me.
I do, Alec—with all my soul. But have mercy on me. I'm not so strong as I thought. It's easy for you to stand alone. You're iron, but I'm a weak woman.
Oh, no, you're not like other women. I was proud of your unconquerable spirit.
It was easy to be brave where my father was concerned, and George, but you're the man I love, and it's so different. I don't know any more how to stand alone.

lg.l: [Alec looks at her, thinking, but does not reply
for a moment.

div.p: Do you remember that only an hour ago I told you that I'd done nothing which I wouldn't do again? I gave you my word of honour that I could reproach myself for nothing.
Oh, I know. I'm so utterly ashamed of myself. But I can't bear the doubt.
Doubt! You've said the word at last.

I tell every one that I don't believe a word of these horrible charges, and I repeat to myself: I'm certain, I'm certain that he's innocent. And yet at the bottom of my heart there's a doubt, and I can't crush it.
Is that why you told them we were engaged to be married?

I wanted to kill that gnawing pain of suspicion. I thought if I stood up before them and cried out that my trust in you was so great, I was willing to marry you notwithstanding everything, I should at least have peace in my own heart.

lg.l: [Alec walks up and down. Then he stops in
front of Lucy.

div.p: What is it precisely you want me to do?

I want you to have mercy on me because I love you. Don't tell the world if you choose not to, but tell me the truth. I know you're incapable of lying. If I only have it from your own lips I shall believe, I want to be certain, certain!

Don't you realise that I would never have asked you to marry me if my conscience hadn't been quite clear? Don't you realise that the reasons I have for holding my tongue must be of overwhelming strength?
But I am going to be your wife, and I love you, and you love me.
I implore you not to insist, Lucy. Let us remember only that the past is gone and we love one another. It's impossible for me to tell you anything.
Oh, but you must now. If any part of the story is true, you must give me a chance of judging for myself.
But you'll kill my love for you. The doubt which lurked at the bottom of my soul now fills me. How can you let me suffer such maddening torture?

I'll be satisfied if you'll only tell me one thing: only tell me that when you sent George on that expedition you didn't know that he'd be killed. [Alec looks at her steadily.] Only say that, Alec. Say that's not true, and I'll believe you.

lg.l: [Lucy does not answer, but stares at him with
terrified eyes.

div.p: Oh, I don't understand. Oh, my dearest, don't treat me as a child. Have mercy on me! You must be serious now. It's a matter of life and death to both of us.
You knew that you were sending George into a death-trap? You knew he couldn't escape alive?
And you don't believe in miracles?
Oh, it can't be true. Oh, Alec, Alec, Alec! Oh, what shall I do?
I tell you that whatever I did was inevitable.
Then if that's true, the rest must be true also. Oh, it's awful. I can't realise it. Haven't you anything to say at all?
[In a low voice.] Only that I've loved you always with all my soul.
You knew how much I loved my brother. You knew how much it meant to me that he should live to wipe out my father's dishonour. All the future was centred on him, and you sacrificed him.

[Hesitatingly.] I think I might tell you this. He had committed a grave error of judgment. We were entrapped by the Arabs, and our only chance of escape entailed the almost certain death of one of us.

lg.l: [An inkling of the truth seizes Lucy, and her

l.hi: face is suddenly distorted with horror. She
goes up to him impulsively. Her voice
trembles with emotion.

div.p: Alec, Alec, he didn't do something—unworthy? You're not trying to shield him?
[With a gasp of relief, almost to herself.] Thank God! I couldn't have borne that. [To Alec, hopelessly.] Then I don't understand.
It was not unjust that he should suffer for the catastrophe which he had brought about.
At those times one doesn't think of justice. He was so young, so frank. Wouldn't it have been nobler to give your life for his?

Oh, my dear, you don't know how easy it is to give one's life. How little you know me! Do you think I should have hesitated if my death had been sufficient to solve the difficulty? I had my work to do. I was bound by solemn treaties to the surrounding tribes. It would have been cowardly for me to die. I tell you, my death would have meant the awful death of every man in my party.
I can only see one thing, that you took George, George of all others.
I knew at the time that what I did might cost me your love, and though you won't believe this, I did it for your sake.

lg.l: [At this moment Mrs. Crowley enters with
Sir Robert Boulger. She has a cloak on.

div.p: I was just coming to say good-night. Bobby is going to drive me home. [She suddenly notices Lucy's agitation.] What on earth's the matter?

lg.l: [Lady Kelsey and Dick Lomas come in. Lady
Kelsey looks at Lucy and then goes up to
her impulsively.

div.p: [Brokenly.] I'm no longer engaged to Mr. Mackenzie. He can't deny that what is said about him is true.

lg.l: [They look at him in astonishment, but he makes

l.hi: no movement.

div.p: [To Alec.] Haven't you anything to say at all? You must have some explanation to offer?
Alec, old man, have you realised all that this means?
Quite. I see now that it was inevitable.
[With a sudden burst of furious anger.] You killed him! You killed him as surely as if you'd strangled him with your own hands.

lg.l: [Robert Boulger goes to the door and flings
it open. Alec gives Lucy a look, then

l.hi: slightly shrugs his shoulders. He walks
out without a word. The moment he has

lg.l: gone Lucy sinks down and bursts into
passionate tears.

div.head: THE FOURTH ACT
div.p: Scene.—A library in the house of Dick Lomas in Portman Square.
Dick and his Valet. Dick is putting flowers into a vase.
Yes, sir. He's gone to his room.
I expect Mrs. Crowley and Miss Allerton to tea. If any one else comes I'm not at home.
And if a caller should ask at what time I'm expected back, you haven't the least idea.
We shall want breakfast at eight to-morrow. I'm going down to Southampton to see Mr. Mackenzie off. But I shall be home to dinner. How about those cases in the hall?
Mr. Mackenzie said they were to be sent for this afternoon. They're only labelled Zanzibar. Is that sufficient, sir?
Oh, I suppose so. Mr. Mackenzie will have given the shippers all directions. You'd better bring the tea at once. Mrs. Crowley is coming at four.

lg.l: [He goes out. Dick continues to arrange the

l.hi: flowers, than goes to the window and looks
out. He comes back. The door is opened by

lg.l: Charles, who announces Mrs. Crowley.

div.p: [Going towards her eagerly and taking both her hands.] Best of women!
You seem quite glad to see me?
I am. But where is Lucy?
She's coming later.... I don't know why you should squeeze my hands in this pointed manner.
What an age it is since I saw you!
If you bury yourself in Scotland all the summer, you can't expect to see people who go to Homburg and the Italian lakes.
It's a sensitive plant whose vagaries one has to humour.
Aren't you delighted to be back in town?
London's the most charming place in the world to get away from and to come back to. Now tell me all you've been doing, if I can hear it without blushing too furiously.
My behaviour would have done credit to a clergyman's only daughter. I dragged Alec off to Scotland after that horrible scene at Lady Kelsey's, and we played golf.
Was he very wretched, poor thing?
He didn't say a word. I wanted to comfort him, but he never gave me a chance. He never mentioned Lucy's name.
No. He was just the same as ever, impassive and collected.
He's an anomaly in this juvenile century. He's an ancient Roman who buys his clothes in Savile Row. An eagle caged with a colony of canaries.
Then he's very much in the way in England, and it's much better for him that he should go back to Africa.
This time to-morrow he'll be half-way down the channel.
I'm really beginning to think you're a perfect angel, Mr. Lomas.
Don't say that, it makes me feel so middle-aged. I'd much sooner be a young sinner than an elderly cherub.
It was sweet of you to look after him through the summer and then insist on his staying here till he went away. How long is he going for this time?
Have you told him that Lucy is coming?
No. I thought that was a pleasing piece of information which I'd leave you to impart.
She's only coming to indulge a truly feminine passion for making scenes, and she's made Alec quite wretched enough already. Why doesn't she marry Robert Boulger?
Half the women I know merely married their husbands to spite somebody else. It appears to be one of the commonest causes of matrimony.
[With a quizzical look at him.] Talking of which, what are you going to do when Mr. Mackenzie is gone?
Talking of the weather and the crops, I propose to go to Spain.
[Opening her eyes wide.] How very extraordinary! I thought of going there, too.
Then, without a moment's hesitation, I shall go to Norway.
Dreadfully. But I shall be supported by the consciousness of having done my duty.
You don't think there would be room for both of us in Spain?
I'm convinced there wouldn't. We should always be running against one another, and you'd insist on my looking out all your trains in Bradshaw.
I hope you remember that you asked me to tea to-day?
Pardon me, you asked yourself. I keep the letter next to my heart and put it under my pillow every night.
You fibber! Besides, if I did, it was only on Lucy's account.
That, I venture to think, is neither polite nor accurate.
I don't think I should so utterly detest you, if you hadn't such a good opinion of yourself.
You forget that I vowed on the head of my maternal grandmother never to speak to you again.
Oh, I'm always doing that. I tell my maid that time she does my hair badly.
You trifled with the tenderest affection of an innocent and unsophisticated old bachelor.
Is that you by any chance?
Of course, it's me. D'you think I was talking of the man in the moon?
[Looking at him critically.] With the light behind, you might still pass for thirty-five.
I've given up youth and its vanities. I no longer pluck out my white hairs.
Then how on earth do you occupy your leisure?
For the last three months I've been laboriously piecing together the fragments of a broken heart.
If you hadn't been so certain that I was going to accept you, I should never have refused. I couldn't resist the temptation of saying "No" just to see how you took it.
I flatter myself that I took it very well.

You didn't. You showed an entire lack of humour. You might have known that a nice woman doesn't marry a man the first time he asks her. It's making oneself too cheap. It was very silly of you to go off to Scotland as if you didn't care.... How was I to know that you meant to wait three months before asking me again?
I haven't the least intention of asking you again.
Then why in heaven's name did you invite me to tea?
May I respectfully remind you, first, that you invited yourself ...
And, secondly, that an invitation to tea is not necessarily accompanied by a proposal of marriage.
I'm afraid you're lamentably ignorant of the usages of good society.
I assure you it's not done in the best circles.
[With a little pout.] I shall be very cross with you in a minute.
Because you're not behaving at all prettily.
D'you know what I'd do if I were you? Propose to me.
Oh, I couldn't do anything so immodest.
I have registered a vow that I will never offer my hand and heart to any woman again.
On the head of your maternal grandmother?
Oh no, far more serious than that. On the grave of my maiden aunt, who left me all my money.
What will you say if I do?
That depends entirely on how you do it. I may remind you, however, that first you go down on your bended knees.
Oh, I waived that with you.
And then you confess you're unworthy of me.

Mr. Lomas, I am a widow. I am twenty-nine and extremely eligible. My maid is a treasure. My dressmaker is charming. I am clever enough to laugh at your jokes, and not so learned as to know where they come from.
Really you're very long-winded. I said it all in four words.
So could I if I might write it down.

But what I'm trying to make you understand is that I don't want to marry you a bit. You're just the sort of man who'll beat his wife regularly every Saturday night.... You will say yes if I ask you, won't you?
I've never been able to refuse a woman anything.
I have no doubt you will after six months of holy matrimony.
I never saw any one make such a fuss about so insignificant a detail as a proposal of marriage.
Dick. [She stretches out her hands, smiling, and he takes her in his arms.] You really are a detestable person.
[With a smile, taking a ring from his pocket.] I bought an engagement ring yesterday on the off chance of its being useful.
Then you meant to ask me all the time?
Of course I did, you silly.
Oh, I wish I had known that before. I'd have refused you again.
[Trying to release herself.] There's somebody coming.
Alec, we've made friends, Mrs. Crowley and I.
It certainly looks very much like it.
The fact is, I've asked her to marry me, and she....
[Interrupting, with a smile.] After much pressure—

I'm so glad. I heartily congratulate you both. I was rather unhappy at leaving Dick, Mrs. Crowley. But now I leave him in your hands, I'm perfectly content. He's the dearest, kindest old chap I've ever known.
Shut up, Alec! Don't play the heavy father, or we shall burst into tears.
He'll be an admirable husband because he's an admirable friend.
I know he will. And I'm only prevented from saying all I think of him and how much I love him, by the fear that he'll become perfectly unmanageable.
Spare me these chaste blushes which mantle my youthful brow. Will you pour out the tea ... Nellie?

lg.l: [She sits down at the tea-table and Dick makes

l.hi: himself comfortable in an arm-chair by

lg.l: her side.

div.p: Well, I'm thankful to say that everything's packed and ready.
I wish you'd stay for our wedding.
Do. You can go just as well by the next boat.
I'm afraid that everything is settled now. I've given instructions at Zanzibar to collect bearers, and I must arrive as quickly as I can.
I wish to goodness you'd give up these horrible explorations.

But they're the very breath of my life. You don't know the exhilaration of the daily dangers—the joy of treading where only the wild beasts have trodden before. Oh, already I can hardly bear my impatience when I think of the boundless country and the enchanting freedom. Here one grows so small, so despicable, but in Africa everything is built to a nobler standard. There a man is really a man; there one knows what are will and strength and courage. Oh, you don't know what it is to stand on the edge of some great plain and breathe the pure keen air after the terrors of the forest. Then at last you know what freedom is.
The boundless plain of Hyde Park is enough for me, and the aspect of Piccadilly on a fine day in June gives me quite as many emotions as I want.
But what will you gain by it all, now that your work in East Africa is over, by all the dangers and the hardships?

Nothing. I want to gain nothing. Perhaps I shall discover some new species of antelope or some unknown plant. Perhaps I shall find some new waterway. That is all the reward I want. I love the sense of power and mastery. What do you think I care for the tinsel rewards of kings and peoples?
I always said you were melodramatic. I never heard anything so transpontine.
And the end of it, what will be the end?
The end is death in some fever-stricken swamp, obscurely, worn out by exposure and ague and starvation. And the bearers will seize my gun and my clothes and leave me to the jackals.
Why, what does it matter? I shall die standing up. I shall go the last journey as I have gone every other.
For all the world like the wicked baronet: Once aboard the lugger and the girl is mine!
Don't you want men to remember you?

Perhaps they will. Perhaps in a hundred years or so, in some flourishing town where I discovered nothing but wilderness, they will commission a second-rate sculptor to make a fancy statue of me. And I shall stand in front of the Stock Exchange, a convenient perch for birds, to look eternally upon the various shabby deeds of human kind.

lg.l: [During this speech Mrs. Crowley makes a sign
to Dick, who walks slowly away and goes
out.

div.p: And is that really everything? I can't help thinking that at the bottom of your heart is something that you've never told to a living soul.

lg.l: [He gives her a long look, and then after a

l.hi: moment's thought breaks into a little smile.

div.p: Why do you want to know so much?

I daresay I shall never see you again. Perhaps it doesn't much matter what I say to you. You'll think me very silly, but I'm afraid I'm rather—patriotic. It's only we who live away from England who really love it. I'm so proud of my country, and I wanted so much to do something for it. Often in Africa I've thought of this dear England, and longed not to die till I had done my work. Behind all the soldiers and the statesmen whose fame is imperishable, there is a long line of men who've built up the Empire piece by piece. Their names are forgotten, and only students know their history, but each one of them gave a province to his country. And I, too, have my place among them. For five years I toiled night and day, and at the end of it was able to hand over to the Commissioners a broad tract of land, rich and fertile. After my death England will forget my faults and my mistakes. I care nothing for the flouts and gibes with which she has repaid all my pain, for I have added another fair jewel to her crown. I don't want rewards. I only want the honour of serving this dear land of ours.
Why is it, when you're so nice really, that you do all you can to make people think you utterly horrid?
Don't laugh at me because you've found out that at heart I'm nothing more than a sentimental old woman.
[Putting her hand on his arm.] What would you do if Lucy came here to-day?

lg.l: [Alec starts, looks at her sharply, then answers
with deliberation.

div.p: I have always lived in polite society. I should never dream of outraging its conventions. If Miss Allerton happened to come, you may be sure I should be scrupulously polite.
Is that all? Lucy has suffered very much.

And do you suppose I've not suffered? Because I don't whine my misery to all and sundry, d'you think I don't care? I'm not the man to fall in and out of love with every pretty face I meet. All my life I've kept an ideal before my eyes. Oh, you don't know what it meant to me to fall in love. I felt that I had lived all my life in a prison, and at last Lucy came and took me by the hand and led me out. And for the first time I breathed the free air of heaven. Oh God! how I've suffered for it! Why should it have come to me? Oh, if you knew my agony and the torture!

lg.l: [He hides his face, trying to master his emotion.
Mrs. Crowley goes to him and puts her
hand on his shoulder.

div.p: [Springing up.] Go away. Don't look at me. How can you stand there and watch my weakness? Oh God, give me strength.... My love was the last human weakness I had. It was right that I should drink that bitter cup. And I've drunk its very dregs. I should have known that I wasn't meant for happiness and a life of ease. I have other work to do in the world. And now that I have overcome this last temptation, I am ready to do it.
But haven't you any pity for yourself, haven't you any thought for Lucy?
Must I tell you, too, that everything I did was for Lucy's sake? And still I love her with all my heart and soul....

lg.l: [She enters, and Dick, anxious that the meeting

l.hi: shall not be more awkward than need be,

lg.l: goes up to her very cordially.

div.p: Ah, my dear Lucy. So glad you were able to come.
[Giving her hand to Dick, but looking at Alec.] How d'you do?
How d'you do? [He forces himself to talk.] How is Lady Kelsey?
She's much better, thanks. We've been to Spa, you know, for her health.
Somebody told me you'd gone abroad. Was it you, Dick? Dick is an admirable person, a sort of gazetteer for polite society.
Won't you have some tea, Lucy?
[Trying on her side also to make conversation.] We shall miss you dreadfully when you're gone, Mr. Mackenzie.

[Smiling.] London is an excellent place for showing one of how little importance one is in the world. One makes a certain figure, and perhaps is tempted to think oneself of some consequence. Then one goes away, and on returning is surprised to discover that nobody has even noticed one's absence.
You're over-modest, Alec. If you weren't, you might be a great man. Now, I make a point of telling my friends that I'm indispensable, and they take me at my word.
You are a leaven of flippancy in the heavy dough of British righteousness.
The wise man only takes the unimportant quite seriously.
[With a smile.] For it is obvious that it needs more brains to do nothing than to be a cabinet minister.
You pay me a great compliment, Alec. You repeat to my very face one of my favourite observations.
[Almost in a whisper.] Haven't I heard you say that only the impossible is worth doing?
Good heavens, I must have been reading the headings of a copy-book.
[To Dick.] Are you going to Southampton to see Mr. Mackenzie off?
I shall hide my face on his shoulder and weep salt tears. It'll be most affecting, because in moments of emotion I always burst into epigram.
I loathe all solemn leave-takings. I prefer to part from people with a nod and a smile, whether I'm going for ever or for a day to Brighton.
Dick has been teaching me to take life flippantly. And I have learnt that things are only serious if you take them seriously, and that is desperately stupid. [To Lucy.] Don't you agree with me?

lg.l: [Her tone, almost tragic, makes him pause

l.hi: for an instant; but he is determined
that the conversation shall be purely conventional.

div.p: It's so difficult to be serious without being absurd. That is the chief power of women, that life and death are merely occasions for a change of costume: marriage a creation in white, and the worship of God an opportunity for a Paris bonnet.

lg.l: [Mrs. Crowley makes up her mind to force a
crisis, and she gets up.

div.p: It's growing late, Dick. Won't you take me round the house?
I'm afraid my luggage has made everything very disorderly.
[To Lucy.] You don't mind if we leave you?

lg.l: [Mrs. Crowley and Dick go out. There is a

l.hi: moment's silence.

div.p: Do you know that our friend Dick has offered his hand and heart to Mrs. Crowley this afternoon?
I hope they'll be very happy. They're very much in love with one another.
[Bitterly.] And is that a reason for marrying? Surely love is the worst possible foundation for marriage. Love creates illusions, and marriages destroy them. True lovers should never marry.
Will you open the window? It seems stifling here.
Certainly. [From the window.] You can't think what a joy it is to look upon London for the last time. I'm so thankful to get away.

lg.l: [Lucy gives a little sob and Alec turns to the

l.hi: window. He wants to wound her and yet
cannot bear to see her suffer.

div.p: To-morrow at this time I shall be well started. Oh, I long for that infinite surface of the clean and comfortable sea.
Are you very glad to go?
[Turning to her.] I feel quite boyish at the very thought.
And is there no one you regret to leave?

You see, Dick is going to marry. When a man does that, his bachelor friends are wise to depart gracefully before he shows them that he needs their company no longer. I have no relations and few friends. I can't flatter myself that any one will be much distressed at my departure.
[In a low voice.] You must have no heart at all.
[Icily.] If I had, I certainly should not bring it to Portman Square. That sentimental organ would be surely out of place in such a neighbourhood.
[Gets up and goes to him.] Oh, why do you treat me as if we were strangers? How can you be so cruel?
[Gravely.] Don't you think that flippancy is the best refuge from an uncomfortable position. We should really be much wiser merely to discuss the weather.
[Insisting.] Are you angry because I came?
That would be ungracious on my part. Perhaps it wasn't quite necessary that we should meet again.

You've been acting all the time I've been here. D'you think I didn't see it was unreal when you talked with such cynical indifference. I know you well enough to tell when you're hiding your real self behind a mask.
If I'm doing that, the inference is obvious that I wish my real self to be hidden.
I would rather you cursed me than treat me with such cold politeness.
I'm afraid you're rather difficult to please.

lg.l: [Lucy goes up to him passionately, but he draws
back so that she may not touch him.

div.p: Oh, you're of iron. Alec, Alec, I couldn't let you go without seeing you once more. Even you would be satisfied if you knew what bitter anguish I've suffered. Even you would pity me. I don't want you to think too badly of me.
Does it much matter what I think? We shall be so many thousand miles apart.
I suppose that you utterly despise me.
No. I loved you far too much ever to do that. Believe me, I only wish you well. Now that the bitterness is past, I see that you did the only possible thing. I hope that you'll be very happy.
Oh, Alec, don't be utterly pitiless. Don't leave me without a single word of kindness.
Nothing is changed, Lucy. You sent me away on account of your brother's death.

lg.l: [There is a long silence, and when she speaks

l.hi: it is hesitatingly, as if the words were
painful to utter.

div.p: I hated you then, and yet I couldn't crush the love that was in my heart. I used to try and drive you away from my thoughts, but every word you had ever said came back to me. Don't you remember? You told me that everything you did was for my sake. Those words hammered at my heart as though it were an anvil. I struggled not to believe them. I said to myself that you had sacrificed George coldly, callously, prudently, but in my heart I knew it wasn't true. [He looks at her, hardly able to believe what she is going to say, but does not speak.] Your whole life stood on one side and only this hateful story on the other. You couldn't have grown into a different man in one single instant. I came here to-day to tell you that I don't understand the reason of what you did. I don't want to understand. I believe in you now with all my strength. I know that whatever you did was right and just—because you did it.
Thank God! Oh, I'm so grateful to you for that.
Haven't you anything more to say to me than that?
You see, it comes too late. Nothing much matters now, for to-morrow I go away.
I'm going to a part of Africa from which Europeans seldom return.
[With a sudden outburst of passion.] Oh, that's too horrible. Don't go, dearest! I can't bear it!
I must now. Everything is settled, and there can be no drawing back.
Don't you care for me any more?
Care for you? I love you with all my heart and soul.
You don't know what I can do. With you to help me I can be brave. Let me come, Alec?
No, it's impossible. You don't know what you ask.
Then let me wait for you? Let me wait till you come back?
And if I never come back?
I will wait for you still.
Then have no fear. I will come back. My journey was only dangerous because I wanted to die. I want to live now, and I shall live.
Oh, Alec, Alec, I'm so glad you love me.

div.head: GENERAL PREFACE
div.p: ...For Clisthenes, son of Aristonymus, son of Myron, son of Andreas, had a daughter whose name was Agarista: her he resolved to give in marriage to the man whom he should find the most accomplished of all the Greeks. When therefore the Olympian games were being celebrated, Clisthenes, being victorious in them in the chariot race, made a proclamation; "that whoever of the Greeks deemed himself worthy to become the son-in-law of Clisthenes, should come to Sicyon on the sixtieth day, or even before; since Clisthenes had determined on the marriage in a year, reckoning from the sixtieth day." Thereupon such of the Greeks as were puffed up with themselves and their country, came as suitors; and Clisthenes, having made a race-course and palæstra for them, kept it for this very purpose. From Italy, accordingly, came Smindyrides, son of Hippocrates, a Sybarite, who more than any other man reached the highest pitch of luxury, (and Sybaris was at that time in a most flourishing condition;) and Damasus of Siris, son of Amyris called the Wise: these came from Italy. From the Ionian gulf, Amphimnestus, son of Epistrophus, an Epidamnian; he came from the Ionian gulf. An Ætolian came, Males, brother of that Titormus who surpassed the Greeks in strength, and fled from the society of men to the extremity of the Ætolian territory. And from Peloponnesus, Leocedes, son of Pheidon, tyrant of the Argives, a decendant of that Pheidon, who introduced measures among the Peloponnesians, and was the most insolent of all the Greeks, who having removed the Elean umpires, himself regulated the games at Olympia; his son accordingly came. And Amiantus, son of Lycurgus, an Arcadian from Trapezus; and an Azenian from the city of Pæos, Laphanes, son of Euphorion, who, as the story is told in Arcadia, received the Dioscuri in his house, and after that entertained all men; and an Elean, Onomastus, son of Agæus: these accordingly came from the Peloponnesus itself. From Athens there came Megacles, son of Alcmæon, the same who had visited Crœsus, and another, Hippoclides, son of Tisander, who surpassed the Athenians in wealth and beauty. From Eretria, which was flourishing at that time, came Lysanias; he was the only one from Eubœa. And from Thessaly there came, of the Scopades, Diactorides a Cranonian; and from the Molossi, Alcon. So many were the suitors. When they had arrived on the appointed day, Clisthenes made inquiries of their country, and the family of each; then detaining them for a year, he made trial of their manly qualities, their dispositions, learning, and morals; holding familiar intercourse with each separately, and with all together, and leading out to the gymnasia such of them as were younger; but most of all he made trial of them at the banquet; for as long as he detained them, he did this throughout, and at the same time entertained them magnificently. And somehow of all the suitors those that had come from Athens pleased him most, and of these Hippoclides, son of Tisander, was preferred both on account of his manly qualities, and because he was distantly related to the Cypselidæ in Corinth. When the day appointed for the consummation of the marriage arrived, and for the declaration of Clisthenes himself, whom he would choose of them all, Clisthenes, having sacrificed a hundred oxen, entertained both the suitors themselves and all the Sicyonians; and when they had concluded the feast, the suitors had a contest about music, and any subject proposed for conversation. As the drinking went on, Hippoclides, who much attracted the attention of the rest, ordered the flute-player to play a dance; and when the flute-player obeyed, he began to dance: and he danced, probably so as to please himself; but Clisthenes, seeing it, beheld the whole matter with suspicion. Afterwards, Hippoclides, having rested awhile, ordered some one to bring in a table; and when the table came in, he first danced Laconian figures on it, and then Attic ones; and in the third place, having leant his head on the table he gesticulated with his legs. But Clisthenes, when he danced the first and second time, revolted from the thought of having Hippoclides for his son-in-law, on account of his dancing and want of decorum, yet restrained himself, not wishing to burst out against him; but when he saw him gesticulating with his legs, he was no longer able to restrain himself, and said: "Son of Tisander, you have danced away your marriage." But Hippoclides answered: "Hippoclides cares not." Hence this answer became a proverb. (Herodotus VI. 126, Cary's Translation.)

div.head: THE FIRST ACT
div.p: Sitting-room of Basil's Lodgings in Bloomsbury.

p.hi: In the wall facing the auditorium, two windows with little iron balconies, giving a view of London roofs. Between the windows, against the wall, is a writing-desk littered with papers and books. On the right is a door, leading into the passage; on the left a fire-place with arm-chairs on either side; on the chimney-piece various smoking utensils. There are numerous bookshelves filled with books; while on the walls are one or two Delft plates, etchings after Rossetti, autotypes of paintings by Fra Angelico and Botticelli. The furniture is simple and inexpensive, but there is nothing ugly in the room. It is the dwelling-place of a person who reads a great deal and takes pleasure in beautiful things.

div.p: Basil Kent is leaning back in his chair, with his feet on the writing-table, smoking a pipe and cutting the pages of a book. He is a very good-looking man of six-and-twenty, clean-shaven, with a delicate face and clear-cut features. He is dressed in a lounge-suit.
[There is a knock at the door.
Yes. I expect a lady to tea. And there's a cake that I bought on my way in.

lg.l: [She goes out, and immediately comes in with a

l.hi: tray on which are two cups, sugar, milk,

div.p: Oh, Mrs. Griggs, I want to give up these rooms this day week. I'm going to be married. I'm sorry to leave you. You've made me very comfortable.
[With a sigh of resignation.] Ah, well, sir, that's lodgers all over. If they're gents they get married; and if they're ladies they ain't respectable.
There's the bell, Mrs. Griggs. I dare say it's the lady I expect. If any one else comes, I'm not at home.

lg.l: [She goes out, and Basil occupies himself for a
moment in putting things in order. Mrs.
Griggs, opening the door, ushers in the
new-comers.
[She goes out again, and during the next few

l.hi: speeches brings two more cups and the tea.

lg.l: [Mabel and Hilda enter, followed by John
Halliwell. Basil going towards them

l.hi: very cordially, half stops when he notices
who they are; and a slight expression of
embarrassment passes over his face. But
he immediately recovers himself and is

lg.l: extremely gracious. Hilda Murray is a

l.hi: tall, handsome woman, self-possessed and

lg.l: admirably gowned. Mabel Halliwell is

l.hi: smaller, pretty rather than beautiful,
younger than her sister, vivacious, very

lg.l: talkative, and somewhat irresponsible.
John is of the same age as Basil, good-humoured,

l.hi: neither handsome nor plain

lg.l: blunt of speech and open.

div.p: Look pleased to see us, Mr. Kent.
You did ask us to come and have tea with you, didn't you?
I've asked you fifty times. Hulloa, John! I didn't see you.
I'm the discreet husband, I keep in the background.
Why don't you praise me instead of praising yourself? People would think it so much nicer.
On the contrary, they'd be convinced that when we were alone I beat you. Besides, I couldn't honestly say that you kept in the background.
[To Basil.] I feel rather ashamed at taking you unawares.
I was only slacking. I was cutting a book.
That's ever so much more fun than reading it, isn't it? [She catches sight of the tea things.] Oh, what a beautiful cake—and two cups! [She looks at him, questioning.]
[A little awkwardly.] Oh—I always have an extra cup in case some one turns up, you know.
How unselfish! And do you always have such expensive cake?
Oh, but I know them well, and I love them dearly. They cost two shillings at the Army and Navy Stores, but I can't afford them myself.
I wish you'd explain why we've come, or Basil will think I'm responsible.
[Lightly.] I've been trying to remember ever since we arrived. You say it, Hilda; you invented it.
[With a laugh.] Mabel, I'll never take you out again. They're perfectly incorrigible, Mr. Kent.
[To John and Mabel, smiling.] I don't know why you've come. Mrs. Murry has promised to come and have tea with me for ages.
[Pretending to feel injured.] Well, you needn't turn me out the moment we arrive. Besides, I refuse to go till I've had a piece of that cake.
Well, here's the tea! [Mrs. Griggs brings it in as he speaks. He turns to Hilda.] I wish you'd pour it out. I'm so clumsy.
[Smiling at him affectionately.] I shall be delighted.

lg.l: [She proceeds to do so, and the conversation goes
on while Basil hands Mabel tea and cake.

div.p: I told them it was improper for more than one woman at a time to call at a bachelor's rooms, Basil.
If you'd warned me I'd have made the show a bit tidier.
Oh, that's just what we didn't want. We wanted to see the Celebrity at Home, without lime-light.
By the way, how is the book?
I always forget to ask how it's getting on.
On the contrary, you never let slip an opportunity of making kind inquiries.
I don't believe you've written a word of it.
Oh, but you're such a monster of discretion.... Now I want to see your medals, Mr. Kent.
Don't be coy! You know I mean the medals they gave you for going to the Cape.
[Gets them from a drawer, and with a smile hands them to Mabel.] If you really care to see them, here they are.
Oh, that's just the common or garden South African medal.
Why didn't they give you the D.S.O.?
Oh, I was only a trooper, you know. They only give the D.S.O. to officers.
And what did you do to deserve it?
It's given for distinguished service in the field, Mabel.
I knew. Only I wanted to see if Mr. Kent was modest or vain.
[With a smile, taking the medals from her and putting them away.] How spiteful of you!
John, why didn't you go to the Cape, and do heroic things?
I confined my heroism to the British Isles. I married you, my angel.
[Laughing.] Are there no more questions you want to ask me, Mrs. Halliwell?
Yes, I want to know why you live up six flights of stairs.
[Amused.] For the view, simply and solely.
But, good heavens, there is no view. There are only chimney-pots.

But they're most æsthetic chimney-pots. Do come and look, Mrs. Murray. [Basil and Hilda approach one of the windows, and he opens it.] And at night they're so mysterious. They look just like strange goblins playing on the house-tops. And you can't think how gorgeous the sunsets are: sometimes, after the rain, the slate roofs glitter like burnished gold. [To Hilda.] Often I think I couldn't have lived without my view, it says such wonderful things to me. [Turning to Mabel gaily.] Scoff, Mrs. Halliwell, I'm on the verge of being sentimental.
I was wondering if you'd made that up on the spur of the moment, or if you'd fished it out of an old note-book.
[With a look at Basil.] May I go out?

lg.l: [Hilda and Basil step out on the balcony,
whereupon John goes to Mabel and tries
to steal a kiss from her.

div.p: Don't be silly. I shall kiss you if I want to.
[She laughing, walks round the sofa while he pursues her.
I wish you'd treat life more seriously.
I wish you wouldn't wear such prominent hats.
[As he puts his arm round her waist.] John, some body'll see us.
Mabel, I command you to let yourself be kissed.
How much will you give me?
[Slipping away from him.] I can't do it for less than half-a-crown.
Now come and sit down quietly.
[Sitting down by his side.] John, you mustn't make love to me. It would look so odd if they came in.
After all, I am your husband.
That's just it. If you wanted to make love to me you ought to have married somebody else. [He puts his arm round her waist.] John, don't, I'm sure they'll come in.
I don't care if they do.
And you won't ever care for anybody else?
[In the same tone.] And you will give me that two-and-threepence, won't you?
Mabel, it was only two shillings.
[Getting up.] I'm going out on the balcony. I'm passionately devoted to chimney-pots.
Isn't it enough for me to say I want you for you to hurl yourself at my feet immediately?
Oh, you poor thing, can't you do without me for two minutes?
Now you're taking a mean advantage. It's only this particular two minutes that I want you. Come and sit by me like a nice, dear boy.
Now what have you been doing that you shouldn't?
[Laughing.] Nothing. But I want you to do something for me.
It's merely to tie up my shoe. [She puts out her foot.]
But, my good girl, it's not undone.
Then, my good boy, undo it and do it up again.
[Starting up.] Mabel, are we playing gooseberry—at our time of life?
[Ironically.] Oh, you are clever! Do you think Hilda would have climbed six flights of stairs unless Love had lent her wings?
I wish Love would provide wings for the chaperons as well.
Don't be flippant. It's a serious matter.
My dear girl, you really can't expect me to play the heavy father when we've only been married six months. It would be almost improper.
It isn't horrid, it's natural history.
[Primly.] I was never taught it. It's not thought nice for young girls to know.
Why didn't you tell me that Hilda was fond of Basil! Does he like her?
I don't know. I expect that's precisely what she's asking him.
Mabel, do you mean to say you brought me here, an inoffensive, harmless creature, for your sister to propose to a pal of mine? It's an outrage.
She's doing nothing of the sort.
You needn't look indignant. You can't deny that you proposed to me.
I can, indeed. If I had I should never have taken such an unconscionably long time about it.
I wonder why Hilda wants to marry poor Basil!
Well, Captain Murray left her five thousand a year, and she thinks Basil Kent a genius.
There's not a drawing-room in Regent's Park or in Bayswater that hasn't got its tame genius. I don't know if Basil Kent is much more than very clever.
Anyhow, I'm sure it's a mistake to marry geniuses. They're horribly bad-tempered, and they invariably make love to other people's wives.
Hilda always has gone in for literary people. That's the worst of marrying a cavalryman, it leads you to attach so much importance to brains.

Yes, but she needn't marry them. If she wants to encourage Basil let her do it from a discreet distance. Genius always thrives best on bread and water and platonic attachments. If Hilda marries him he'll only become fat and ugly and bald-headed and stupid.
Why, then he'll make an ideal Member of Parliament.
[Basil and Hilda come into the room again.
[Maliciously.] Well, what have you been talking about?
[Acidly.] The weather and the crops, Shakespeare and the Musical Glasses.
It's getting very late, Mabel. We really must be going.
[Getting up.] And I've got to pay at least twelve calls. I hope every one will be out.
People are so stupid, they're always in when you call.
[Holding out her hand to Basil.] Good-bye.
[Coldly.] Thanks so much, Mr. Kent. I'm afraid we disturbed you awfully.
[Shaking hands with her.] I've been enchanted to see you. Good-bye.
[Lightly.] We shall see you again before you go to Italy, shan't we?
Oh, I'm not going to Italy now, I've changed all my plans.
[Giving John a look.] Oh! Well, good-bye. Aren't you coming, John.
No: I think I'll stay and have a little chat with Basil, while you tread the path of duty.
Well, mind you're in early. We've got a lot of disgusting people coming to dinner.
[With a smile.] Poor things! Who are they?
I forget who they are. But I know they're loathsome. That's why I asked them.
[Basil opens the door, and the two women go out.

[Sitting down and stretching himself.] Now that we've got rid of our womankind let's make ourselves comfortable. [Taking a pipe out of his pocket.] I think I'll sample your baccy if you'll pass it along.
[Handing him the jar.] I'm rather glad you stayed, John. I wanted to talk to you.

lg.l: [Basil pauses a moment, while John looks at

l.hi: him with amusement. He fills his pipe.

div.p: [Lighting his pipe.] Nice gal, Hilda—ain't she?
[Enthusiastically.] Oh, I think she's perfectly charming.... But what makes you say that?
[Innocently.] Oh, I don't know. Passed through my head.
I say, I've got something to tell you, John.
Well, don't be so beastly solemn about it.

No, it ain't. I've done it myself. It's like a high dive. When you look down at the water it fairly takes your breath away, but after you've done it—it's not so bad as you think. You're going to be married, my boy.
[With a smile.] How the deuce d'you know?
[Gaily.] Saw it with mine own eyes. I congratulate you, and I give you my blessing. I'll get a new frock-coat to give the lady away in.
You?... [Suddenly understanding.] You're on the wrong tack, old man. It's not your sister-in-law I'm going to marry.
Then why the dickens did you say it was?
H'm! I've made rather more than an average ass of myself, haven't I?
What on earth made you think...?
[Interrupting.] Oh, it was only some stupid idea of my wife's. Women are such fools, you know. And they think they're so confoundedly sharp.
No, of course not! Well, who the deuce are you going to marry?
[Flushing.] I'm going to marry Miss Jenny Bush.
Never heard of her. Is it any one I know?
[Searching his memory.] Bush ... Bush.... [With a smile.] The only Jenny Bush I've ever heard of was a rather pretty little barmaid in Fleet Street. Presumably you're not going to marry her.

[John has said this quite lightly, not guessing for a moment that it can have anything to do with the person Basil proposes to marry. Then, since Basil makes no answer, John looks at him sharply: there is a silence while the two men stare at one another.
Basil, it's not the woman we used to know before you went out to the Cape?
[Pale and nervous, but determined.] I've just told you that you used to know Jenny.
Man alive, you're not going to marry the barmaid of the "Golden Crown"?
[Looking at him steadily.] Jenny was a barmaid at the "Golden Crown."
But, good Lord, Basil, what d'you mean? You're not serious?
Perfectly! We're going to be married this day week.
Are you stark, staring mad? Why on earth d'you want to marry Jenny Bush?
That's rather a delicate question, isn't it? [With a smile.] Presumably because I'm in love with her.
Well, that's a silly ass of an answer.

Nonsense! Why, I've been in love with twenty girls, and I haven't married them all. One can't do that sort of thing in a country where they give you seven years for bigamy. Every public-house along the Thames from Barnes to Taplow is the tombstone of an unrequited passion of my youth. I loved 'em dearly, but I never asked 'em to marry me.
[Tightening his lips.] I'd rather you didn't make jokes about it, John.
Are you sure you're not making an ass of yourself? If you've got into a mess, surely we can get you out. Marriage, like hanging, is rather a desperate remedy.
[Basil is sitting down and moodily shrugs his shoulders. John goes up to him, and putting his hands on his friend's shoulders looks into his eyes.
Why are you going to marry her, Basil?
[Springing up impatiently.] Damn you, why don't you mind your own business?
Can't I marry any one I choose? It's nothing to you, is it? D'you suppose I care if she's a barmaid?
[He walks up and down excitedly, while John with steady eyes watches him.
Basil, old man, we've known each other a good many years now. Don't you think you'd better trust me?
[Setting his teeth.] What d'you want to know?
Why are you going to marry her?
[There is a silence. Then Basil, more calmly turns to John.
Yes, rather. Why, we always lunched there in the old days.

Well, after I came back from the Cape I began going there again. When I was out there she took it into her head to write me a letter, rather ill-spelt and funny—but I was touched that she thought of me. And she sent some tobacco and some cigarettes.
My maiden aunt sent you a woollen comforter, but I'm not aware that in return you ever made her a proposal of marriage.
And so in one way and another I came to know Jenny rather well. She appeared to get rather fond of me—and I couldn't help seeing it.
But she always pretended to be engaged to that scrubby little chap with false teeth who used to hang about the bar and make sheep's eyes at her over innumerable Scotch-and-sodas.
He made a scene because I took her out on one of her off-nights, and she broke it off. I couldn't help knowing it was on my account.
After that I got into the habit of taking her to the play, and so on. And finally...!
How long has this been going on?
Well, the other day she wired for me. I found her in the most awful state. She was simply crying her eyes out, poor thing. She'd been seedy and gone to the doctor's. And he told her ...
What you might really have foreseen.
Yes.... She was quite hysterical. She said she didn't know what to do nor where to go. And she was in an awful funk about her people. She said she'd kill herself.
[Drily.] Naturally she was very much upset.
I felt the only thing I could do was to ask her to marry me. And when I saw the joy that came into her poor, tear-stained face I knew I'd done the right thing.
[There is a pause. John walks up and down, then stops suddenly and turns to Basil.
Have you thought that you, who've never needed to economise, will have to look at every shilling you spend? You've always been careless with your money, and what you've had you've flung about freely.
[Shrugging his shoulders.] If I have to submit to nothing worse than going without a lot of useless luxuries, I really don't think I need complain.
But you can't afford to keep a wife and an increasing family.
I suppose I can make money as well as other men.
I shall set to work to earn my living at the Bar. Up till now I've never troubled myself.
I don't know any man less fit than you for the dreary waiting and the drudgery of the Bar.
And what d'you think your friends will say to your marrying—a barmaid?
[Contemptuously.] I don't care two straws for my friends.

That's pleasant for them. You know, men and women without end have snapped their fingers at society and laughed at it, and for a while thought they had the better of it. But all the time society was quietly smiling up its sleeve, and suddenly it put out an iron hand—and scrunched them up.
[Shrugging his shoulders.] It only means that a few snobs will cut me.
I'm not such a cad as to go to a house where I can't take my wife.

But you're the last man in the world to give up these things. There's nothing you enjoy more than going to dinner-parties and staying in country houses. Women's smiles are the very breath of your nostrils.

You talk of me as if I were a tame cat. I don't want to brag, John, but after all, I've shown that I'm fit for something in this world. I went to the Cape because I thought it was my duty. I intend to marry Jenny for the same reason.
[Seriously.] Will you answer me one question—on your honour?
Are you in love with her?
[Passionately.] Then, by God, you have no right to marry her. A man has no right to marry a woman for pity. It's a cruel thing to do. You can only end by making yourself and her entirely wretched.
I can't break the poor girl's heart.

You don't know what marriage is. Even with two people who are devoted to one another, who have the same interests and belong to the same class, it's sometimes almost unbearable. Marriage is the most terrible thing in the world unless passion makes it absolutely inevitable.
My marriage is absolutely inevitable—for another reason.
You talk as if such things had never happened before.
Oh, I know, they happen every day. It's no business of the man's. And as for the girl, let her throw herself in the river. Let her go to the deuce, and be hanged to her.
Nonsense. She can be provided for. It only needs a little discretion—and no one will be a ha'porth the wiser, nor she a ha'porth the worse.
But it's not a matter of people knowing. It's a matter of honour.
[Opening his eyes.] And where precisely did the honour come in when you...?
Good heavens, I'm a man like any other. I have passions as other men have.
[Gravely.] My dear Basil, I wouldn't venture to judge you. But I think it's rather late in the day to set up for a moralist.

D'you think I've not regretted what I did? It's easy enough afterwards to say that I should have resisted. The world would be a Sunday School if we were all as level-headed at night as we are next morning.
[Shaking his head.] After all, it's only a very regrettable incident due to your youth and—want of innocence.
[With vehement seriousness.] I may have acted like a cur. I don't know. I acted as I suppose every other man would. But now I have a plain duty before me, and, by God, I mean to do it.

Don't you realise that you've only one life and that mistakes are irreparable? People play with life as if it were a game of chess in which they can try this move and that, and when they get into a muddle, sweep the board clear and begin again.
But life is a game of chess in which one is always beaten. Death sits on the other side of the board, and for every move he has a counter-move. And for all your deep-laid schemes he has a parry.

But if at the end Death always mates you, the fight is surely worth the fighting. Don't handicap yourself at the beginning by foolish quixotry. Life is so full. It has so much to offer, and you're throwing away almost everything that makes it worth the trouble.
[Gravely.] Jenny would kill herself if I didn't marry her.
You don't seriously think she'd do that. People don't commit suicide so easily, you know.

You've thought of a great deal, John—you've not thought of the child. I can't let the child skulk into the world like a thief. Let him come in openly and lawfully. And let him go through the world with an honest name. Good heavens, the world's bad enough without fettering him all his life with a hideous stigma.
[Interrupting.] You can bring forward a thousand objections, but nothing alters the fact that, under the circumstances, there's only one way open to a man of honour.
[Drily.] Well, it's a way that may do credit to your heart, but scarcely to your understanding.
I thought you'd see at once that I was doing the only possible thing.

My dear Basil, you talk of pity, and you talk of duty, but are you sure there's anything more in it than vanity? You've set yourself up on a sort of moral pinnacle. Are you sure you don't admire your own heroism a little too much?
[With a good-natured smile.] Does it look so petty as that in your eyes? After all, it's only common morality.

[Impatiently.] But, my dear chap, its absurd to act according to an unrealisable ideal in a world that's satisfied with the second-rate. You're tendering bank-notes to African savages, among whom cowrie shells are common coin.
[Smiling.] I don't know what you mean.

Society has made its own decalogue, a code that's just fit for middling people who are not very good and not very wicked. But Society punishes you equally if your actions are higher than its ideal or lower.
Sometimes it makes a god of you when you're dead.
But it takes precious good care to crucify you when you're alive.
[There is a knock at the door, and Mrs. Griggs comes in.
Show 'em in. [To John] It's Jenny. She said she was coming to tea.
[With a smile.] Oh, the cake was for her, was it? Would you like me to go?
Not unless you choose. Do you suppose I'm ashamed?
I thought, after all you've told me, you might not care for me to see her.

[Jenny Bush and her brother James come in. She is very pretty, with delicate features and a beautiful complexion: her fair hair is abundant and very elaborately arranged. She is dressed smartly, rather showily. It is the usual type of barmaid, or tea-girl, a shade more refined perhaps than the common run. Her manners are unobjectionable, but not those of a gentlewoman. James is a young man with clean-shaven face and a sharp expression. He is over-dressed in a very horsey manner, and is distinctly more vulgar than his sister. He talks English with a cockney accent, not invariably dropping his aitches, but only now and then. He is over cordial and over genial.
[Going up to Basil.] I'm awfully late, I couldn't come before.
[Jocosely.] Don't mind me. Give 'im a kiss, old tart.
Oh, I brought my brother Jimmie to see you.
Nicely, thanks. Pleased to make your acquaintance.
[Looking at John and suddenly recognising him.]
Well, I never! If that isn't old John Halliwell. I didn't expect to see you. This is a treat.
I've been having a cup of tea with Basil.
[Looking at the tea-things.] D'you always drink out of three cups at once?
My wife has been here—and her sister.
Oh, I see. Fancy your being married. How d'you like it?
[Basil pours out a cup of tea, and during the following speeches gives Jenny milk and sugar and cake.
People say it wants a bit of gettin' used to.
Well, I will say this for myself, you'd want to get up early in the morning to catch me nappin'. I didn't catch your name.
That's what I say—'Alliwell. I knew a fellow in the meat trade called 'Alliwell. Any relation?
Fine business 'e 'ad too. There's a rare lot of money to be made out of meat.
[To John.] It is a long time since I've seen you. I suppose you've quietened down now you're a married man. You were a hot 'un when you was a bachelor.
[Facetiously.] Don't make 'im blush, Jenny. Accidents will 'appen in the best regulated families. And boys will be boys, as they say in the Bible.
I think I must be off, Basil.
Well, I'll be toddlin' too. I only come in just to say 'ow d'you do to my future brother-in-law. I'm a fellow as likes to be cordial. There's no 'aughtiness about me.
[Politely, but not effusively.] Oh; won't you stay and have some tea?
No, thanks. I'm not much of an 'and at tea; I leave that to females. I like something stronger myself.
I have some whisky, Mr. Bush.

Oh, blow the Mister and blow the Bush. Call me Jimmie. I can't stand ceremony. The way I look on it is this. We're both of us gentlemen. Now, mind you, I'm not a fellow to praise myself. But I will say this: I am a gentleman. That's not self-praise, is it?
Dear me, no. Mere statement of fact.

Well, as I was saying, I know I'm a gentleman. It's a thing you can't 'elp, so what's the good of being proud about it? If I meet a chap in a pub, and he invites me to have a drink, I don't ask him if he's a Lord.
Well, you'd do the same yourself, wouldn't you?
I dare say. But will you have a drink now?

Oh, bless you, I know what it is to be engaged. I don't want to disturb you canary-birds. Me and 'Alliwell 'll go and have a gargle round the corner. I see you've got a public nice and 'andy. [To John.] I suppose you're not above goin' in there now and again, eh?
[With a laugh.] He came into the "Golden Crown" every day of his life, and chance it!
I'm afraid I'm in a great hurry.
'Ang it all, one's always got time to have a drop of Scotch in this life.
[To James, handing him the box.] Well, take a cigar with you.
[Taking and examining one.] If you are so pressing. Villar y Villar.... What do they run you in a hundred?
They were given to me, I really don't know what they cost. [He lights a match.] Won't you take the label off?
Not if I know it. I don't smoke a Villar y Villar every day, but when I do, I smoke it with the label on.
[Shaking hands with Jenny.] Good-bye and—my best wishes.
Thanks. You didn't expect I'd marry Basil when I used to mix cocktails for you in the "Golden Crown," did you?
Come on, 'Alliwell. Don't stop there gassing. You'll only disturb the canary-birds. So long, old tart, see you later. Ta-ta, Basil, old man.
[John Halliwell and James go out, Jenny goes up to Basil impulsively.
Kiss me. [He kisses her, smiling.] There! Now I can sit down quietly and talk. How d'you like my brother?
Oh—I hardly know him yet. He seems very amiable.
He's not a bad sort when you know him. He's just like my mother.
[Raising his brows.] Is he? And—is your father like that too?
Well, you know, Pa hasn't had the education that Jimmie's had. Jimmie was at a boarding-school at Margate.
You were at a boarding-school, too, weren't you?
Ah, you don't get the fine air at Harrow that you get at Margate.
Shall I put down your cup?
[Placing it on a table.] Oh, thanks, it's all right. Come and sit by me, Basil.
[Seating himself on the arm of her chair.] There.
[Taking his hand.] I'm so glad we're alone. I should like to be alone with you all my life. You do love me, don't you, Basil?
I'm so glad. Oh, I don't know what I should do if you didn't love me. If you hadn't been kind to me I should have thrown myself in the river.
[He passes his hand affectionately over her hair.
Oh, you are so good, Basil. I'm so proud of you. I shall be so proud to be your wife.
[Gravely.] Don't think too well of me Jenny.
[With a laugh.] I'm not afraid of that. You're brave and you're clever and you're a professional man, and you're everything.
[Passionately.] I can't tell you how much I love you.
I'll try with all my might to be a good husband to you, Jenny.

lg.l: [She flings her arms round his neck and they

l.hi: kiss one another.

div.head: THE SECOND ACT
div.p: An Interval of One Year Elapses Between Acts I. and II.

The drawing-room in Basil's house at Putney. In the wall facing the auditorium there is a door leading from the passage. On the right two doors lead into bedrooms, and opposite these is a bay window. The same pictures and plates decorate the walls as in the preceding Scene; the writing-table is between the side doors. Jenny's influence is noticeable in the cushions in the wicker-work arm-chairs, in the window curtains and portières of art serge, and in the huge chrysanthemums of the wall paper.

lg.l: [Jenny is sewing while James Bush is lounging
in one of the arm chairs.

div.p: He's gone out for a walk.
[With a malevolent laugh.] That's what he tells you, my dear.
[Looking up quickly.] Have you seen him anywhere?
No, I can't say I 'ave. And if I 'ad I wouldn't boast about it.
Well, whenever I come here he's out for a walk.... I say, old tart, could you oblige me with a couple of sovereigns till next Saturday?
[Pained to refuse.] Oh no, Jimmie, I can't manage it. Basil made me promise I wouldn't let you have any more.
What! He made you promise that?—Ugh, the mean skinflint.
We've lent you so much, Jimmie. And ma's had a lot, too.
Well, look here, you can manage a sovereign, can't you? You needn't say anything about it.
I can't really, Jimmie. I would if I could. But we've got a rare lot of debts worrying us, and the rent will be coming along next week.
